rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وزيد بن أرقم
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd and Zayd ibn Arqam report that they used to speak during prayer, return greetings, and ask about the number of rakʿas; the command to stand qunūtān ordered silence and forbade speech.
rows.anchor: وهو قول ابن مسعود وزيد بن أرقم : كنا نتكلم في الصلاة فيسلم الرجل فيردون عليه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid explains qunūt as humility, lowered bearing, still limbs, avoiding distraction out of awe of God, and remaining free of worldly thoughts during prayer.
rows.anchor: وهو قول مجاهد : القنوت عبارة عن الخشوع ، وخفض الجناح وسكون الأطراف

rows.speaker: قائلون
rows.claim: Some explain qunūt as standing, understanding the phrase as standing for a long time.
rows.anchor: هو القيام ، واحتجوا عليه بحديث جابر قال

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Jābir reports that, when asked which prayer is best, the Prophet answered that it is the one with lengthy qunūt, meaning lengthy standing.
rows.anchor: سئل النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم : ( أي الصلاة أفضل ؟ قال طول القنوت )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī considers the standing interpretation weak because it would make the verse say, redundantly, to stand standing; it works only if qunūt means continuing the standing.
rows.anchor: وهذا القول عندي ضعيف ، وإلا صار تقدير الآية : وقوموا لله قائمين

rows.speaker: علي بن عيسى
rows.claim: ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā takes qunūt to mean persistence, patience, and adherence; in religious usage it is persistence in obeying and serving God.
rows.anchor: وهو اختيار علي بن عيسى : أن القنوت عبارة عن الدوام على الشيء والصبر عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says this broad sense encompasses the other commentators' explanations and may mean persisting in standing whenever standing is obligatory or recommended.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون المراد : وقوموا لله مديمين على ذلك القيام في أوقات وجوبه واستحبابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After requiring preservation of prayer with its pillars and conditions, God limits that full observance to times of safety rather than fear.
rows.anchor: هذه المحافظة على هذا الحد لا تجب إلا مع الأمن دون الخوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase is also transmitted with rāʾ vowelled ḍamma, with a doubled rāʾ, or in the singular form rajulā.
rows.anchor: بضم الراء و { رجالا } بالتشديد و { رجلا }

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī takes the fear to be fear of an enemy, with the object of the verb omitted because context makes it understood.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي رحمه الله معنى الآية : فإن خفتم عدوا فحذف المفعول لإحاطة العلم به

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf allows fear of an enemy or any other cause; al-Rāzī prefers this because the concession applies whenever fear occurs.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب الكشاف : فإن كان بكم خوف من عدو أو غيره ، وهذا القول أصح

rows.speaker: قول ثالث
rows.claim: A third interpretation is fear that prayer time will expire if prayer is delayed until the fighting ends.
rows.anchor: وفيه قول ثالث وهو أن المعنى : فإن خفتم فوات الوقت إن أخرتم الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the time-expiration reading, the verse underscores the obligation to pray within its prescribed time, permitting concessions to preserve it.
rows.anchor: الآية تدل على تأكيد فرض الوقت حتى يترخص لأجل المحافظة عليه بترك القيام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rijālan is the plural of rājil, someone on foot, whether walking or standing still; the source lists several plural forms.
rows.anchor: رجالا جمع راجل مثل تجار وتاجر وصحاب وصاحب والراجل هو الكائن على رجله ماشيا كان أو وافقا

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffāl allows rijāl to be a plural of a plural, deriving it through the plural forms of rājil.
rows.anchor: ما ذكره القفال ، وهو أنه يجوز أن يكون جمع الجمع ، لأن راجلا يجمع على راجل

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Rukbān is the plural of rākib; al-Qaffāl says rākib is used for someone on a camel, while a person on a horse is called fāris.
rows.anchor: والركبان جمع راكب ، مثل فرسان وفارس ، قال القفال : ويقال إنه إنما يقال راكب لمن كان على جمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rijālan is an accusative circumstantial expression whose governing verb is omitted; the implied wording is “pray on foot or riding.”
rows.anchor: رجالا نصب على الحال ، والعامل فيه محذوف ، والتقدير : فصلوا رجالا أو ركبانا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fear prayer has two settings: during fighting, addressed here, and outside fighting, addressed in the prayer-of-fear passage in al-Nisāʾ.
rows.anchor: صلاة الخوف قسمان أحدهما : أن تكون في حال القتال وهو المراد بهذه الآية والثاني : في غير حال القتال

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī permits prayer in joined battle on foot or mounted, facing or away from the qibla, with gestures for bowing and prostration, making the latter lower and avoiding needless shouts.
rows.anchor: فمذهب الشافعي رحمه الله أنهم يصلون ركبانا على دوابهم ومشاة على أقدامهم

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa says a person on foot does not pray in this situation but delays the prayer.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حنيفة : لا يصلي الماشي بل يؤخر

rows.speaker: ابن عمر ونافع
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar understands the phrase to permit facing or not facing the qibla; Nāfiʿ says he believes Ibn ʿUmar received this from the Prophet.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عمر : { فرجالا أو ركبانا }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī argues that severe fear makes it impossible to keep facing the qibla or safely stand for full bowing and prostration, so the wording permits turning away and gesturing.
rows.anchor: لا يمكن معه المحافظة على الاستقبال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer still requires intention and recitation; extraneous speech and unnecessary cries remain forbidden.
rows.anchor: فعل القلب وهو النية ، وذلك لا يسقط لأنه لا يتبدل حال الخوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Standing and sitting fall away, while gestures replace bowing and prostration; the gesture for prostration should be lower than the one for bowing.
rows.anchor: وأما الركوع والسجود فالإيماء قائم مقامهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Purification does not lapse because water or earth can be used; al-Rāzī prefers allowing tayammum with dust while mounted when water is present but unsafe to use, since danger to life outweighs fear of thirst.
rows.anchor: وأما ترك الطهارة فغير جائز لأجل الخوف ، فإنه يمكنه التطهير بالماء أو التراب

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī cites the Prophetic instruction to perform of a commanded act whatever one is able to do as the basis for the Shāfiʿī position.
rows.anchor: إذا أمرتكم بشيء فأتوا منه ما استطعتم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa argues that the Prophet delayed prayer on the day of the Trench, so Muslims should do likewise.
rows.anchor: واحتج أبو حنيفة بأنه عليه السلام أخر الصلاة يوم الخندق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī answers that the danger at the Trench did not reach the severity described here, so this verse abrogated the Prophet's earlier delay.
rows.anchor: لم يبلغ الخوف هذا الحد ومع ذلك فإنه صلى الله عليه وسلم أخرى الصلاة فعلمنا كون هذه الآية ناسخة لذلك الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fear prayer applies in battle and outside it; battle may be obligatory, permitted, or prohibited. Fighting unbelievers is the original case, and fighting rebels is included by the command in 49:9.
rows.anchor: أما القتال الواجب فهو كالقتال مع الكفار وهو الأصل في صلاة الخوف ، وفيه نزلت الآية

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو المحاسن الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Qāḍī Abū al-Maḥāsin al-Ṭabarī says defending oneself is permitted rather than obligatory, except when an unbeliever targets the person, when defense is obligatory to protect Islam's rights.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي أبو المحاسن الطبري في كتاب شرح المختصر : أن دفع الإنسان عن نفسه مباح غير واجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fear prayer is permitted when defending oneself or any animal whose life is protected.
rows.anchor: أما القتال في الدفع عن النفس وفي الدفع عن كل حيوان محترم ، فإنه يجوز فيه صلاة الخوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jurists differ over defending property: al-Rāzī prefers permitting fear prayer, reasoning from the report that one killed defending property is a martyr, which equates its defense with self-defense.
rows.anchor: فيه قولان : الأصح أن يجوز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opposing view denies the property-defense concession, reasoning that the sanctity of another protected interest is greater.
rows.anchor: والثاني : لا يجوز لأن حرمة الزوج أعظم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The concession does not apply to prohibited fighting: it would assist wrongdoing, and a sinful aggressor does not merit such assistance.
rows.anchor: أما القتال المحظور فإنه لا تجوز فيه صلاة الخوف ، لأن هذا رخصة والرخصة إعانة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Outside battle, the concession applies to someone fleeing fire, flood, or a predatory animal, and to an insolvent debtor fearing detention who cannot prove insolvency, because the wording is general.
rows.anchor: أما الخوف الحاصل لا في القتال ، كالهارب من الحرق والغرق والسبع وكذا المطالب بالدين إذا كان معسرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the wording may suggest battle, the verse establishes the concession to prevent harm, and that rationale also applies to noncombat dangers.
rows.anchor: إلا أنه لما ثبت هناك دفعا للضرر ، وهذا المعنى قائم ههنا ، فوجب أن يكون ذلك الحكم مشروعا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that prayer was prescribed as four rakʿas at home, two while traveling, and one during fear.
rows.anchor: روي عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنه أنه قال : فرض الله على لسان نبيكم الصلاة في الحضر أربعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority require four rakʿas at home and two on a journey whether or not there is fear; they regard Ibn ʿAbbās's view as abandoned.
rows.anchor: والجمهور على أن الواجب في الحضر أربع ، وفي السفر ركعتان سواء كان في الخوف أو لم يكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the fear that occasioned the concession ends, “remember God” means perform prayer as taught and prescribed; the ordinary duty returns, and prayer is called remembrance in 62:9.
rows.anchor: فاذكروا بمعنى فافعلوا الصلاة كما علمكم

rows.speaker: قول ثان
rows.claim: A second interpretation takes remembrance of God to mean thanking Him for granting safety.
rows.anchor: أي فاشكروه لأجل إنعامه عليكم بالأمن

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qāḍī objects that this conditional remembrance should be specific to safety; gratitude is due during fear as well, since both conditions contain God's blessings and the fear comes from unbelievers, not God.
rows.anchor: طعن القاضي في هذا القول وقال : إن هذا الذكر لما كان معلقا بشرط مخصوص

rows.speaker: قول ثالث
rows.claim: A third interpretation includes both prayer and gratitude, with gratitude specifically due upon safety and performed alongside prayer at its appointed times.
rows.anchor: القول الثالث : أنه دخل تحت قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “As He taught you” recalls God's favor in teaching and guiding people; without His guidance they would not have reached this knowledge.
rows.anchor: فبيان إنعامه علينا بالتعليم والتعريف ، وأن ذلك من نعمه تعالى ، ولولا هدايته لم نصل إلى ذلك

rows.speaker: أصحابنا والمعتزلة
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī's Ashʿarite colleagues explain the teaching as God creating knowledge, while the Muʿtazila explain it as furnishing proofs and acts of grace.
rows.anchor: ثم إن إصحابنا فسروا هذا التعليم بخلق العلم والمعتزلة فسروه بوضع الدلائل ، وفعل الألطاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What people did not know points to the era before Muḥammad's mission, a time of ignorance and error.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى ما قبل بعثة محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم من زمان الجهالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first appeal to “our Lord” recalls that God nurtured the speaker before he professed monotheism, and asks how divine generosity could now abandon him after a life of monotheism.
rows.anchor: حين ما لم أذكرك بالتوحيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second appeal contrasts being nurtured while nonexistent, when neglect could not harm, with the severe harm that would follow neglect now.
rows.anchor: ربيتني حين كنت معدوما ، ولو لم تربني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third appeal makes God's past nurturing an intercessor for continued nurturing in the future.
rows.anchor: فاجعل لي في الماضي شفيعي إليك في أن تربيني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fourth appeal asks God to complete past kindness, since completing a favor is better than beginning one.
rows.anchor: ورابعها : ربيتني في الماضي فإتمام المعروف خير من ابتدائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The declaration of return affirms resurrection alongside belief in God's beginning of creation: whoever recognizes God's knowledge of particulars and power over all possible things must affirm the return.
rows.anchor: بيان أنهم كما أقروا بالمبدأ فكذلك أقروا بالمعاد ، لأن الإيمان بالمبدأ أصل الإيمان بالمعاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Knowing one must return to God, whose judgment alone rules and whose permission is required for intercession, makes obedience more sincere and avoidance of sins more complete.
rows.anchor: كان إخلاصه في الطاعات أتم ، واحترازه عن السيئات أكمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī closes this passage by marking the end of the Qurʾān's account of the believers' faith.
rows.anchor: وهاهنا آخر ما شرح الله تعالى من إيمان المؤمنين

words: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says the opening clause may be God's own statement or a continuation of the believers' words following their confession and prayer in 2:285.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن يكون ابتداء خبر من الله ويحتمل أن يكون حكاية عن الرسول والمؤمنين

words: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the believers speak the clause, it follows their “we hear and obey”: since God mercifully requires only what is within capacity, they must respond with obedience as servants.
rows.anchor: فكأنهم قالوا : كيف لا نسمع ولا نطيع

words: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If God speaks the clause, it answers the believers' plea for forgiveness: after their obedience and request for pardon over deliberate shortcomings, He reassures them about inadvertent lapses.
rows.anchor: فهذا إجابة لهم في دعائهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb is used in the construction “I burdened him with a thing, so he undertook it”; taklīf is its verbal noun.
rows.anchor: يقال : كلفته الشيء فتكلف ، والكلف اسم منه

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ treats wusʿ as a noun, like wajd and juhd.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : هو اسم كالوجد والجهد

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Others define capacity as what a person can bear without constriction or hardship, below the utmost degree of exertion.
rows.anchor: الوسع ما يسع الإنسان ولا يضيق عليه ولا يحرج فيه

words: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazila cite this verse and 22:78, 4:28, and the promise of ease to argue that God does not impose what a person cannot do.
rows.anchor: المعتزلة عولوا على هذه الآية في أنه تعالى لا يكلف العبد ما لا يطيقه

words: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: Their first premise is that people create their own acts: if God created the commanded act, the person could neither produce it again nor resist God's power; if God did not, the person could not bring it about.
rows.anchor: الأول : أن العبد موجد لأفعال نفسه ، فإنه لو كان موجدها هو الله تعالى

words: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: Their second premise is that ability precedes the act; otherwise an unbeliever commanded to believe would not be able to do so, making the command impossible.
rows.anchor: والثاني : أن الاستطاعة قبل الفعل وإلا لكان الكافر المأمور بالإيمان لم يكن قادرا على الإيمان

words: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī's Ashʿarite colleagues say rational proofs establish that impossible commands do occur, so this verse must be interpreted.
rows.anchor: أما الأصحاب فقالوا : دلت الدلائل العقلية على وقوع التكليف على هذا الوجه

words: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first rational argument invokes God's eternal knowledge that one who dies in unbelief will never believe; that foreknown nonbelief is incompatible with belief, making the command appear to require a contradiction and likewise raising the problem of compulsion.
rows.anchor: من مات على الكفر ينبىء موته على الكفر أن الله تعالى كان عالما في الأزل بأنه يموت على الكفر

words: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second argument says acts depend on motives created by God; if motives instead came from the person, an infinite regress follows, while a determining motive makes the alternative impossible, yet the unbeliever is commanded to believe.
rows.anchor: لأن قدرة العبد لما كانت صالح للفعل والترك

words: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third argument says a command issued when motives are equal requires contradictory equality and preference; if one motive prevails, the preferred is necessary and the other impossible.
rows.anchor: فإن كان الأول فهو تكليف ما لا يطاق ، لأن الاستواء يناقض الرجحان

words: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fourth argument says Abū Lahab was commanded to believe even though God had announced that he would not believe, so he was required to believe that he would not believe.
rows.anchor: أنه تعالى كلف أبا لهب الإيمان

words: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fifth argument says people do not know the detailed count of movements and rests in an act such as moving a finger; since they did not intend that precise count, they do not create it, and an undetermined preference is impossible.
rows.anchor: العبد غير عالم بتفاصيل فعله ، لأن من حرك أصبعه لم يعرف عدد الأحيان التي حرك أصبعه فيها

words: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī deems the rational proofs decisive: when they conflict with an apparent scriptural meaning, one must preserve the proofs and interpret the apparent text, or undermine rational grounds for monotheism, prophecy, and scripture.
rows.anchor: لم يبق إلا أن يقطع بصحة الدلائل العقلية ، ويحمل الظاهر السمعي على التأويل

words: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī notes that the same interpretive method is routinely used by the Muʿtazila against anthropomorphic readings; thus the verse certainly admits interpretation even if its precise interpretation is left unspecified.
rows.anchor: وهذا الكلام هو الذي تعول المعتزلة عليه أبدا في دفع الظواهر التي تمسك بها أهل التشبيه

words: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second answer defines command as notice that action brings reward and omission brings punishment; where an act is impossible, the statement is not a real command but notice of punishment and one's creation for Hell.
rows.anchor: لا معنى للتكليف في الأمر والنهي إلا الإعلام بأنه متى فعل كذا فإنه يثاب

words: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
rows.speaker: طائفة من قدماء أهل الجبر
rows.claim: A group of early determinists says people are commanded while it remains unknown whether God knows they will die unbelievers; after such a death, one learns the obstacle was present and the condition for obligation had been absent during life.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول طائفة من قدماء أهل الجبر

words: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth answer says the clause is spoken by the believers and therefore does not prove God's rule; al-Rāzī calls this weak, since God recounts and praises their words, so they must be truthful.
rows.anchor: إلا أن هذا ضعيف ، وذلك لأن الله تعالى لما حكاه عنهم في معرض المدح لهم والثناء عليهم

words: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī ends this dispute by asking God to show mercy to their incapacity and limited understanding and forgive their errors, affirming that they seek only truth.
rows.anchor: فإنا لا نطلب إلا الحق ، ولا نروم إلا الصدق

words: لَهَا مَا كَسَبَتْ وَعَلَيْهَا مَا ٱكْتَسَبَتْ
rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī says the language treats kasb and iktisāb as synonyms; Dhū al-Rummah's verse and Qurʾānic uses interchange them in 74:38, 6:164, 2:81, and 33:58.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي رحمه الله : الصحيح عند أهل اللغة أن الكسب والاكتساب واحد لا فرق بينهما

words: لَهَا مَا كَسَبَتْ وَعَلَيْهَا مَا ٱكْتَسَبَتْ
rows.speaker: بعض الناس
rows.claim: Some accept a distinction: kasb can be for oneself or another, while iktisāb is only what one acquires for oneself; one can be a breadwinner for one's family but not an acquirer for them.
rows.anchor: ومن الناس من سلم الفرق ، ثم فيه قولان أحدهما : أن الاكتساب أخص من الكسب

words: لَهَا مَا كَسَبَتْ وَعَلَيْهَا مَا ٱكْتَسَبَتْ
rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf says good is called kasb and evil iktisāb because evil is desired by the commanding soul, which works harder to acquire it, whereas the good term does not imply such exertion.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) : إنما خص الخير بالكسب
